summary: Describes the problems with spanning tree protocols in IEEE 802.1 LANs, such as strict loop avoidance and unused alternate paths. It then explains the problem and applicability of TRILL, which brings routing to bridging, and the situations suited to it.

plainLanguage.summary: Old networks block extra roads to avoid traffic loops, wasting them. This note explains why using smarter route finding in those networks can make use of the extra roads.

questions: why is spanning tree a problem
what are the benefits of link layer routing
subtitle: Routing protocols at the link layer to overcome spanning tree limitations.

tldr.problem: Spanning tree protocols in Ethernet LANs strictly prevent loops but block alternate paths, waste bandwidth, converge slowly, and can lose multicast traffic during topology changes.
tldr.mechanism: TRILL applies modern network-layer routing protocols at the link layer, allowing traffic to use multiple efficient paths while still supporting Ethernet's plug-and-play simplicity.
tldr.outcome: TRILL solutions maintain Ethernet's backward compatibility and zero-configuration properties while enabling better use of available bandwidth and faster convergence after link failures.

facts.label: Problem scope
facts.value: Single Ethernet link subnet (up to ~1000 end-hosts per bridged LAN)

facts.label: Ring topology with N bridges
facts.value: STP forces N-1 hop paths; routing allows 1 hop

today: RFC 5556 is an Informational RFC that described the problem and applicability of TRILL. RFC 7780 (Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links: Clarifications, Corrections, and Updates) later provided updates, and RFC 6326 specified the actual TRILL protocol.

sections.title: The Problem: Spanning Trees vs. Routing
sections.content:
Ethernet networks use spanning tree protocols to prevent broadcast loops: they automatically disable redundant links to create a single tree through all bridges. This simplicity comes with a cost. Traffic is forced onto the tree path even when shorter paths exist. When the tree changes, reconvergence can take 30 seconds or more, during which traffic may be lost. Modern routing protocols at layer 3 avoid these problems by using each available link efficiently and converging rapidly, but they require devices to renumber when they move to a different network.

TRILL (Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links) asks: what if we brought routing's efficiency to the link layer, while keeping Ethernet's ability for devices to move without renumbering?
sections.plainLanguage: Ethernet networks draw a single tree and forbid the other roads, to avoid loops. TRILL lets you use all the roads the way routers do, but still keeps the simple plug-and-play that Ethernet users expect.

sections.title: Core Problems with Spanning Tree
sections.content:
The Spanning Tree Protocol (STP) creates efficiency problems. In a ring of N bridges, STP blocks one link and forces traffic between nodes on either side of the blocked link to traverse N-1 hops around the ring. A modern routing protocol would forward that traffic in one hop across the direct link. Even worse, STP limits bandwidth: all traffic flows across a single tree backbone, concentrating load on a few links and leaving others idle.

STP also struggles with convergence. When a link fails, especially one attached to the root bridge, many ports must block and unblock as the tree recalculates. Old STP implementations can wait 30 seconds before traffic flows again. Newer variants (RSTP, MSTP) are faster but still slower than link-state routing. Additionally, STP is global across the entire link-layer subnet; there is no way to partition it into smaller, more stable regions the way Internet routing partitions Autonomous Systems.

Finally, when bridges snoop on IP multicast control messages to optimize multicast forwarding, topology changes can cause multicast traffic to be misdirected and lost until new control messages arrive.
sections.plainLanguage: Spanning tree blocks roads and forces all traffic down one path. If the tree changes, it can take a long time for traffic to find a new path, and multicast can get lost.

sections.title: What TRILL Solutions Need to Do
sections.content:
A TRILL solution must solve these routing and convergence problems while maintaining full backward compatibility with existing Ethernet. This means supporting broadcast, multicast, and unicast just as bridges do, preserving the in-order delivery of frames between the same pair of link addresses, and supporting VLANs. New devices must discover and organize themselves with zero configuration and zero assumptions about the network topology, just as hubs and bridges do.

TRILL solutions also need to handle forwarding loops. Link-state routing protocols can create transient loops during convergence, so TRILL must detect and mitigate them—either by decrementing a hop count (like IP TTL), by tracking visited nodes, or by checking for traffic on unexpected interfaces. The solution must participate gracefully in spanning tree management without requiring changes to existing STP protocols. It must support multiple attachments to avoid creating loops when a node or segment connects to multiple TRILL components.

Finally, TRILL solutions should not interfere with Internet protocols. The IP TTL field cannot be co-opted for loop mitigation since the Internet assumes unchanged TTL across a link-layer subnet. Broadcast and multicast must work transparently across TRILL deployments.
sections.plainLanguage: TRILL devices must look like smart Ethernet bridges to each other and to old devices. They need to find each other automatically, route traffic efficiently, stop loops, and handle multiple connections without creating tangles.

sections.title: Where TRILL Applies
sections.content:
TRILL solutions address path efficiency, concentration, multipathing, and stability within a single Ethernet link subnet. Like bridges, TRILL components aggregate into a single TRILL solution within a subnet. TRILL is not intended to span separate subnets interconnected by routers, except via link-layer tunnels that make the distinct subnets look like one.

TRILL solutions do not address scalability beyond current IEEE 802.1 bridged LANs (around 1,000 end-hosts in a single bridged LAN or 100,000 hosts across 1,000 VLANs served by 10,000 bridges). They also do not tackle other Ethernet challenges such as host migration, security vulnerabilities like spoofing or flooding, or ARP issues. Solutions should not introduce new security vulnerabilities compared to traditional bridging, but they are not expected to be a general fix for Ethernet security problems.
sections.plainLanguage: TRILL works within one Ethernet network to solve routing problems. It is not meant to connect different subnets or fix all Ethernet security issues.

sections.title: A Concrete Example
sections.content:
Consider a bridged network with eight bridges arranged such that each bridge connects to several others. A spanning tree selects a root bridge and creates a tree by enabling one link between each pair of branches. Traffic from host A (on bridge A) to host C (on bridge C) travels A→B→H→E→C, using the tree path. Simultaneously, traffic from G to F travels G→H→E→F, also on the tree.

Both flows share the H-E link. If each link has 100 Mbps, the combined bandwidth for both flows is capped at 100 Mbps because they compete for H-E. With routing, traffic from G to F could use the direct G-F link, leaving H-E available for A-C traffic. The same network could then support 200 Mbps total, with each flow at full capacity. This is the core benefit TRILL aims to recover: using network topology more efficiently and reducing bottlenecks.
sections.plainLanguage: With spanning tree, two separate conversations might be forced to share one road. With routing at the link layer, they can each take their own path.
